\end{aligned}
$$

$$
6a - 30b=\frac{6}{5}(5a - 25b).

$$
λ=\frac{6}{5}
$$

The two non-zero vectors are parallel. Their directions are the same because the factor is positive.

Use the parametrized line-integral formula:
$$

Substitute $x=t\sin t$ and $y=t\cos t$:
$$
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))
=t\sin t\,\mathbf i+(t\cos t-1)\,\mathbf j.
$$
Both coordinates require the product rule:
$$
\mathbf r'(t)=(\sin t+t\cos t)\,\mathbf i
+(\cos t-t\sin t)\,\mathbf j.
$$
Take the dot product and expand:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r'(t)
&=t\sin t(\sin t+t\cos t)\\
&\quad +(t\cos t-1)(\cos t-t\sin t)\\
&=t\sin^2t+t^2\sin t\cos t\\
&\quad +t\cos^2t-t^2\sin t\cos t\\
&\quad -\cos t+t\sin t\\
&=t-\cos t+t\sin t.
\end{aligned}
$$
The mixed terms cancel, but the offset in the field leaves two extra terms. To integrate them, note that
$$
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}(-t\cos t)=-\cos t+t\sin t.
$$
Thus
$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r
&=\int_0^\pi(t-\cos t+t\sin t)\,\mathrm dt\\
&=\left[\frac{t^2}{2}-t\cos t\right]_0^\pi\\
&=\frac{\pi^2}{2}-\pi(-1)-0\\
&=\frac{\pi^2}{2}+\pi.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate
$$
\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r,
$$
where $\mathbf F(x,y,z)=x\,\mathbf i+z\,\mathbf j+y\,\mathbf k$ and $C$ is the path
$$
\mathbf r(t)=-\sin t\,\mathbf i+\sec t\,\mathbf j+\cos t\,\mathbf k,\qquad 0\le t\le\frac\pi4.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use
$$
\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r=\int_0^{\pi/4}\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r'(t)\,\mathrm dt.
$$
Along the curve, $x=-\sin t$, $y=\sec t$, and $z=\cos t$. Therefore
$$
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))=-\sin t\,\mathbf i+\cos t\,\mathbf j+\sec t\,\mathbf k.
$$
Differentiate each curve component, keeping both negative signs:
$$
\mathbf r'(t)=-\cos t\,\mathbf i+\sec t\tan t\,\mathbf j-\sin t\,\mathbf k.
$$
Take the dot product before integrating:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r'(t)&=(-\sin t)(-\cos t)\\
&\quad+\cos t\sec t\tan t-\sec t\sin t\\
&=\sin t\cos t+\tan t-\tan t\\
&=\sin t\cos t.
\end{aligned}
$$
The second and third terms cancel since $\cos t\sec t=1$ and $\sec t\sin t=\tan t$. Finally,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r&=\int_0^{\pi/4}\sin t\cos t\,\mathrm dt\\
&=\left[\frac12\sin^2t\right]_0^{\pi/4}\\
&=\frac12\left(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)^2-0=\frac14.
\end{aligned}
$$
